entry.title: Lift of the replay progress bar class: three of four verified methods
entry.summary: From lane l-cls23.
entry.content:
From lane l-cls23.

Asked. Lift the verified methods of the replay progress bar class to portable Rust, each proven against its verified 32-bit rewrite.

Found.

ItemFactStatus
Update method extentThe inventory size runs into the next routine. The routine ends with a return 373 bytes in; the verified rewrite was proven over that extent.Verified
Draw method extentThe routine is 4,095 bytes; the inventory says 4,089.Verified
Teardown routine nameIts inventory name says constructor; it is the teardown the deleting destructor calls first. Its rewrite comment says menu-state object, which does not match the class.Verified for the call pattern; Inferred for the class
Update contractThe first out-word of the first fill call is never written by the contract, so it is zero on every trial. The narrowing list records only the zeroed stack fill.Verified from the contract

Decided. Lift the deleting destructor, the teardown and the update, which together cover the class's lifecycle and per-frame behaviour. Defer the draw method: it orders floating-point work through helpers, keeps a local frame array and reads nine globals, and its lift needs float-exact output checks. The four unverified methods are not lifted.

Result. Six differential tests pass on the 32-bit target, 3,000 seeded trials per method, and 13 deliberately wrong lifts are caught. Twelve host tests pass on the 64-bit host. The lifted module has no unsafe blocks.

Reproduce. Run the lane's differential test crate on the 32-bit target with one test thread, and its host tests on the 64-bit host. Each method's registry row names its rewrite and its test.

Limits. The proofs script the collaborators, do not verify them, and do not compare stack words. Each row of the registry lists what its proof does not cover.

entry.title: Lifting the go-to-point-on-route task family: eight of nine verified methods proven
entry.summary: Verified. Lane l-cls24 lifted eight of the nine verified methods of the go-to-point-on-route task class into portable Rust. Each lifted method runs against its verified 32-bit rewrite on 20,000 generated cases: the return value, every byte of the task object, the output words, the shared cache and the ordered log of every call with its arguments. All eight pass; a deliberately wrong lift of each method is caught by the same cases.
entry.content:
Verified. Lane l-cls24 lifted eight of the nine verified methods of the go-to-point-on-route task class into portable Rust. Each lifted method runs against its verified 32-bit rewrite on 20,000 generated cases: the return value, every byte of the task object, the output words, the shared cache and the ordered log of every call with its arguments. All eight pass; a deliberately wrong lift of each method is caught by the same cases.

Verified. The class has two virtual tables that carry its methods, and the same rewrites appear under the parent class's tables. A slot number names a method only together with its table.

Decision. The route follow step (the largest verified method of the family, with eleven callees and shared counters) is not lifted in this lane. Six listed methods have no verified rewrite and were left out rather than written from their names.

Verified. Several verified rewrites write constants that the original reads from its own data (a zero, an upper clamp bound, a blend weight and a helper's argument). The values agree today, but the proofs cannot see a change to those words; the rule that a value loaded from the image is loaded in the rewrite is not met by these.

Verified. One rewrite's comment names a flag mask that does not match its code, and another carries a placeholder phrase in place of a description. One contract declares a word that its rewrite never reads, so that declaration is inert.

Unknown. Whether the route updater, the allocator and the scale helper behave as the lifted host contracts describe on the real game: they are the test's scripted stand-ins, and the lift states what each proof narrows.

entry.title: Layout frame of the interface toolkit: 37 of 38 verified methods lifted and proven
entry.summary: From lane l-cls20.
entry.content:
From lane l-cls20.

Asked. Lift the verified methods of the front end's base widget class (the layout frame) from their 32-bit rewrites into portable Rust that owns its data, and prove each lifted method against its rewrite on the 32-bit target.

Found (Verified). The class has 96 named methods; 38 are verified. Thirty-seven of the verified methods are proven here. The one left out is a single forwarded engine call with no behaviour of its own. Of the 37, 25 call nothing (field stores, byte masks, two block copies, and two branches on a field). The other 12 call out: the token follow-up family (resolve a token, run the frame's own step, hand the answer to a target step), a clamped blend that forwards to the frame's handler, a record-flag query, an indexed-list check, a pointer-list release, and a parameter-block refresh. The 58 unverified methods are not lifted.

GroupMethodsWhat they share
Stores and masks21One field each, written through named offsets; byte setters keep the low byte and answer it
Copies and branches4Two 24-byte block copies; a tag compare; a fill-once cache word
Token family7Resolve, frame step, target step; shared flags and object read and cleared through a host
Blend, queries, list, parameter block5Single-precision blend with pinned operand order; host-supplied records, list entries and block words

Decided. The lifted frame is an owned block of the bytes the methods touch, with offsets named by what they hold. Methods that call out take a host trait for their callees and collaborators, and the host reports every call; the proofs compare the calls in order with their arguments. Nothing reads the operating system. The one allocator the family uses is a host trait. A method whose rewrite answers its own address is restated with the answer narrowed to the input, and the narrowing is listed per method in the registry.

How it is proven. A test crate includes the verified rewrite files unchanged and runs each lifted method against its rewrite on generated frames, floats compared by their bits. Each method also has a deliberately wrong lift, which the same trials must catch. A separate host-side test set covers the edge cases: the empty branches, the order of calls, and the fallbacks. Nothing here is checker-verified; the lifted methods are proven against verified rewrites.

Limits. Shared flags and list records are compared by their final values, not by the order of their reads. The allocation-failure path of one method is not run, because the original writes through the null block there. The dossier's names for the callees are proposed and were not used.

entry.title: Scene-draw render phase verified on one rewrite, with a caller survey behind its return value
entry.summary: From lane a-H44.
entry.content:
From lane a-H44.

Asked: finish the scene-draw render-phase method left partly proven by an earlier lane, and show whether its return register matters to any caller. Found: one rewrite passes twenty-two contracts at 1000 trials each on the stock checker, covering every branch and all nineteen callees; eight deliberately wrong versions each fail 1000 of 1000 trials on a second library. The caller survey found that the method is held by one vtable slot and has no direct caller in the code section; every call through that slot on a render-phase receiver discards the return register; five call sites read the register but have receivers of other classes by owner and calling pattern (Inferred); two call sites sit in the encrypted first megabyte and cannot be decoded (Unknown). Decided: publish as verified with the return register listed as a narrowing, because the project rule accepts a narrow proof that says what it does not cover.

Surprise: the earlier lane's table of call arguments missed that a float store overwrites a pushed register slot before one call, and that the answers of three callees are used rather than discarded. Both are handled correctly in the published rewrite and its contracts.

entry.title: Lifting the follow-point route task: all ten verified methods
entry.summary: From lane l-cls21.
entry.content:
From lane l-cls21.

What was asked: turn the verified 32-bit rewrites of the follow-point route task (a ped walks a route of points, one leg at a time) into portable Rust that owns its data, and prove each lifted method against its rewrite. What is reported: all ten verified methods lifted and proven; the five unverified methods listed and not written.

What the family looks like

The task keeps a route table (a count, then one entry per point), a waypoint index, a flag word and a cursor. Its methods pick the closest route segment for a ped, step the route on when a sub-task ends, copy points out of the tables, construct and clone the task, release it, and poll the owner once per step. The construction and clone paths call a move-base constructor and a route constructor; the poll calls the owner and the sub-task through their own virtual tables. Two verified rewrites read the same word of the task (its eighth byte) as two different objects, and one word is read both as a route index and as a handle. Both are recorded as open questions, not resolved here.

What was lifted and how it is proven

One state record owning the task's data, a host trait for every call the task makes on the outside (the task system, the owners, the sub-tasks, the allocator, the release context), and each verified method as a method. The proof builds real 32-bit memory for each rewrite, runs the rewrite and the lifted method on the same inputs, and compares the results, every host call in order with its arguments, the written fields and bytes, and floats bit for bit. Nine differential tests pass on the 32-bit target, and nine tests check that seventeen deliberately wrong lifts are caught; twenty-four host tests pass on the 64-bit host. The lifted module has no unsafe code and no addresses.

What is still missing

Five methods are unverified and not written. The host traits need real implementations in the port: the constructors' move base and route builder, the task system, the sub-task factory, the owner objects and the helpers. Narrowings are recorded per method: out-pointer answers become values, the sub-task type query is compared as answers rather than as a count, vtable words are the class's identity and not represented, and the poll's count clear drops entries past the count.

entry.title: Game camera class lifted: five verified methods proven against their rewrites
entry.summary: From lane l-cls22.
entry.content:
From lane l-cls22.

2026-10-12

Asked. Lift the game camera class from its verified 32-bit rewrites into portable Rust, with a differential proof for each method that has behaviour in it.

Found. Seven methods are listed for the class. Five have verified rewrites; all five are now lifted and proven. Two listed entries have no size and no rewrite and were left out. The five cover the deleting destructor, the restart, the camera event step, the blend update and the idle reset.

MethodWhat it does (lifted name)CalleesWrong versions caught
Deleting destructorRuns the destructor body; returns storage to the pool when the low flag bit is set21 of 1
RestartTears down, builds a worker, chains and releases it, clears the active marker and pending words2 plus 2 virtual2 of 2
Camera event stepTwo gate blocks around a middle chain, then the tail165 of 5
Blend updateFour updates, the initialised marker, two blend channels while the singleton exists, two updates114 of 4
Idle resetClears the mode, timer and flag words, sets the idle marker and the default zoom12 of 2

Method. Each lifted method runs against its verified rewrite on 2000 generated camera images. The comparison covers the return, every camera word, every global, and every collaborator call in order; floats compare bit for bit, with NaN payloads and boundary values in the generated inputs. Each method also has deliberately wrong versions, and each was caught on at least one trial. The runtime is test-only; the lifted code has no unsafe code. Nothing here is verified by the checker: the claim is agreement with the verified rewrites on the generated inputs.

Finding. The comment on the blend update's rewrite gives the counter step as n plus three times n divided by three. The verified arithmetic gives the remainder of the count, read as a signed value, after division by three. A host check agrees with the remainder for every count from zero to 200000 and for the negative words. The lifted code keeps the original's sequence, so the proof is unaffected; the comment needs correcting.

Not done. The two undecoded entries; two slots with no rewrite in the family list, whose meaning is not established. The bodies behind the class's collaborator interface (destructor body, reset step, gate provider, watcher, sink, singleton, update steps, tail provider) are unlifted callees: a port must implement each of them.

Source. The verified rewrite files for the five methods, read as rewrites and compared against the lifted code. Results are recorded in the lane's results file for the coordinator's re-run.

entry.title: Eight operating faults in one evening, all made by the coordinator while it was improving the pipeline
entry.summary: Between 20:00 on 11 October and 00:05 on 12 October the coordinator changed the brief, the checker's driver, the importer, the re-run rules and 488 published files, and made eight mistakes doing it. None of them put a wrong function into the verified set for longer than two minutes, and none lost verified work. Each cost time, three of them broke the public pipeline, and one was a false report to the owner. This entry lists them together because they have one cause.
entry.content:
Between 20:00 on 11 October and 00:05 on 12 October the coordinator changed the brief, the checker's driver, the importer, the re-run rules and 488 published files, and made eight mistakes doing it. None of them put a wrong function into the verified set for longer than two minutes, and none lost verified work. Each cost time, three of them broke the public pipeline, and one was a false report to the owner. This entry lists them together because they have one cause.

What was asked

The verified set grew at its best rate at thirty lanes that evening. Why did the coordinator, which writes no game code, produce more faults in four hours than the lanes did, and what changes?

The faults

FaultEffectHow it was found
Two patches put new paragraphs into the brief makers' string literals with single backslashes. When a maker ran, the language read a backslash and the letter after it in several folder names as a carriage return, a form feed or a vertical tab.Every brief generated for about three hours named its output folders with control characters in the middle. Most lanes worked out the intended names; one wrote its contracts under a misspelt folder.A lane's output folder had a name that matched nothing, and its brief was then read back.
The checker's driver gained a check that refuses a contract which places a value inside code. The pipeline pins the driver's hash, and the pin was not moved.The pipeline failed on the next commit.The pipeline's own failure message.
The same check imported two analysis libraries at the top of its file. The pipeline's machines do not install them; the driver only needs them when it is given a game image.The pipeline failed a second time, on the commit that fixed the pin.The pipeline's failure message. The imports now happen inside the one function that uses them.
The formatter was run on the whole workspace. Lift test crates include verified rewrites by path, and the formatter follows those paths.Seven tracked files were reformatted, four of them verified rewrites whose text is part of their proof record.The list of changed files after the run. The seven were restored unchanged, and path modules now carry a marker the formatter respects.
488 published files that did not build alone were replaced by repaired files. Each repaired file had been built alone and run against its contract of record. No crate that includes verified files was built with them.One older lift test crate supplied a constant that a repaired rewrite now defines for itself, and stopped building. The lift tests failed in the pipeline. The repair also took two commits where one was meant, because the list of paths assumed one folder.The hourly scorecard showed the pipeline as failing.
The coordinator told the owner that the pipeline run measuring the repair had passed. It had read the run's manifest of the assembled library, which was the number it wanted, and had not read the run's conclusion.A false report, and three lift commits pushed onto a failing pipeline before it was noticed.The same scorecard. The statement was corrected in chat and in the changelog, and the crate was fixed after all 80 lift test crates were built to look for other collisions of the kind. There were none.
A lane claimed two functions and the re-run could repeat only one. The coordinator wrote the hold on the other by hand, in a form the importer does not read, and imported the lane.The function whose proof could not be repeated was in the verified index for under two minutes. It is not known to differ from the original.By the coordinator, straight after the import. The function was taken out and the hold rewritten in the importer's form.
The importer and the re-run script were each patched in place through a shell that rewrote characters in the patch.Each script was unable to run for about twenty seconds, while the finishers that call them were running.Seen at once, and each file was restored from its backup. The check that the patched file parses had been left until after it was written.

Smaller slips of the same evening: two changelog entries with a wrong count, corrected by follow-up entries, and two status headings whose time was written from memory of the last one.

False holds are a separate account

Over the same hours the coordinator's re-run held good claims because its rules for pairing a proof with its wrong version were narrower than what lanes actually write: a wrong version under the same export name, in a folder of another name, with a different seed, or declared inside the proof's own contract. More than sixty claims were recovered as the rules were widened, and the brief now prescribes one layout. These erred on the safe side, since a held claim is not counted, and they are listed here only because the widening of those rules was a large part of the evening's rate of change.

What was established

  • The cause is the coordinator's rate of change. Every one of the eight is a change that was made and put into use in one step, with its check either missing or run afterwards. The lanes work under a brief that makes them prove a thing before they claim it; the coordinator was not holding its own tools to that.
  • The verified set was protected by the parts that did not change that evening: the stock checker, the re-run of every claim before import, and the hold on anything the re-run cannot reproduce. The one function that got past did so on a hold written by hand.
  • The scorecard, which reads the pipeline's conclusion from the service and not from the coordinator's memory, caught the false report within the hour. That is what it is for.

What was decided

  • A script is patched on a copy. The copy must parse, and no string in it may contain a control character, before it replaces the script in use.
  • Text inserted into another script's source contains no backslash and no brace, or is inserted with both escaped and read back through the language's own rules first.
  • A pipeline run is reported as passing only from its conclusion, with the list of jobs that did not pass printed beside it.
  • Before a change to verified files is committed, every crate that includes verified files is built.
  • The formatter is run on named packages, never on the workspace.
  • A hold is written with the script that writes holds, never by hand.
  • Fewer changes to the pipeline per hour, each validated before the next. The lanes do not need the coordinator to move at the speed it was moving.

How to check it

The changelog for 11 and 12 October carries an entry for each fault and for each correction, titled by what it changed; the pipeline's history for the same hours shows the three failures and the runs that followed them. The hourly review row for 00:05 on 12 October gives the coordinator's own ranking of these faults at the time.

entry.title: Lifting a render phase: the mirror reflection, four methods proven
entry.summary: From lane l-cls18.
entry.content:
From lane l-cls18.

What was asked: turn the four verified 32-bit rewrites of the mirror-reflection render phase class into portable Rust that owns its data, and prove each lifted method against its rewrite on generated cases, with a deliberately wrong copy of each method that the cases must catch.

What was found (Verified): all four verified methods are lifted and proven. The class's object keeps a target handle, a parameter-block handle, three filter seeds and a status byte. Its process-wide values are a set of gates, flags, a three-word-per-entry parameter table and a stamp counter. Every other call goes to a collaborator the phase does not own, and only one virtual slot is called at all. Semantic names for the four methods follow their slot and behaviour (Inferred); the meanings of the numbered collaborator calls are not established (Unknown) and are named by role only.

How the lift is shaped

One trait holds every collaborator call of the four methods, in the original's argument order. Object references are named by offset from the phase or the scene snapshot, or are opaque handles. The phase's own words are a struct with load and store at named offsets. Process-wide values are one state value the caller owns. No address, numbered slot or unsafe block appears in the lifted module.

How it is proven

Each case builds the object, its parameter block, the snapshot, the query blocks and the globals in one memory image, runs the rewrite, restores the image and runs the lift on the same bytes. Results, every recorded call with its arguments and pointer contents, and the whole final image must agree. Inputs are widened on purpose: counts at the signed limits, every gate combination, not-a-number and infinity patterns in float words, and table words anywhere. Each method's wrong copy (one changed line) is caught in some cases. On the 32-bit target, 4,000 cases per method agree.

A finding about the phase's own words (Verified)

The first draft of the lift held the phase's target and parameter handle for the whole call. A scripted rebuild that writes those two words, which the original then reads again, was caught by the cases: the draft differed. The lift now re-reads the two words after each call it makes with the phase or one of its members. A copy without that re-read is caught in 130 of 400 cases. What remains unproven: a collaborator that is given neither the phase nor one of its members, and writes its words anyway, is assumed not to exist (Unknown whether any does).

What the verified proofs cover less than the lift does

Two of the verified contracts declare full-image comparison off, and one sets the unused-stack fill to zero. The lift's proof compares the full image and every callee argument, so on those points it is the stronger of the two (Verified from the contracts; the rewrites themselves were not re-proven).

entry.title: Base sound class (audSound family) lifted: nine verified methods proven against their rewrites
entry.summary: From lane l-cls16.
entry.content:
From lane l-cls16.

12 October 2026

Asked. Lift the base class of the audio engine's sounds, the interface every kind of sound implements, from its verified 32-bit rewrites into portable Rust, and prove each lifted method against its rewrite on the same generated inputs.

Found. The class has a nine-slot virtual table. Nine of the thirteen listed methods are verified and lifted: the second constructor, the deleting destructor, the lookups by hash and by name, the store and forwarding helpers, the link forwarding method, the attach method and the advance method. The always-false slot is verified but has no behaviour to lift. The default constructor and the two playback-time getters have no verified rewrite yet.

ItemValueMeaning
Methods lifted and proven9 of 13Each against its verified rewrite, 300 generated cases
Wrong versions caught9 of 9Each lifted method has one deliberately wrong copy; each is caught
Host tests20 passEdge cases on the 64-bit host against a scripted world
Differential tests19 passNine proofs and nine wrong lifts, on the 32-bit target
Unsafe in lifted code0The module forbids unsafe code; the test runtime alone allows it

How the proof works. The lifted method and the verified rewrite run in one test memory at real 32-bit addresses. The check compares the return value, every engine call in order with its arguments, and every byte of the memory afterwards. Engine globals, numbered callees and virtual slots sit behind one trait; the lifted code calls it with the original's arguments in the original's order.

Narrowed. The proofs cover what the test memory can hold: voice rows are limited to the first five, the init table to its first 44 entries, and the attached voice's scratch frame is recorded by position only. The advance routine's proof covers divisor entries from 3 to 7, because the rewrite has no timer wait for entries 0 to 2 and its contract pins them to three or more.

Decided. The lifted methods make no operating-system call. Every engine interaction is a trait method, so a port implements it over its own object model. The advance routine's timer wait is not in the verified rewrite and is not in the lift.

Checks for the coordinator. Two verified contracts (the attach and advance routines) set the stack fill to zero. The advance rewrite's own comment says it defines an uninitialised word below the stack as zero, which is the pattern the stack-fill rule warns about. The advance routine's evidence entry also lists five callees that its rewrite does not call. Neither was resolved in this lane.

Reproduce. From the lane's tree: the host tests with cargo test on the lf-audio crate's sound_base_host test; the differential tests with cargo test on the lf-soundbase-diff crate for the i686-pc-windows-msvc target, with two test threads (about one minute).

entry.title: Hourly reviews, 12 October
entry.summary: The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour, from its own timer, on the checklist the owner supplied, starting from a scorecard a script prints: verified code in bytes per hour that held on the coordinator's own re-run is the measure, lifts are counted separately, and every exception the scorecard lists is acted on in the same hour. One row is added here per review. The day before's rows are in "Hourly reviews, 11 October".
entry.content:
The coordinator reviews the project critically once an hour, from its own timer, on the checklist the owner supplied, starting from a scorecard a script prints: verified code in bytes per hour that held on the coordinator's own re-run is the measure, lifts are counted separately, and every exception the scorecard lists is acted on in the same hour. One row is added here per review. The day before's rows are in "Hourly reviews, 11 October".

What was asked

To check every hour that the project is going in the right direction and to improve the process from what was just learned.

What was found

TimeMain findingDecision
00:05The best hour of verified code at thirty lanes, a repair of 488 published files measured, and a pipeline the coordinator broke with that repair and wrongly reported as passing. Between 23:02 and 00:04: verified code up by 20,556 bytes in 248 functions (19,893 bytes an hour, against 14,141 over the last 24 hours); 42 routines lifted, to 1,311. Luna lanes that ended in the hour verified 265 functions and 20,340 bytes in 30 lane-hours, with six claims held. Nothing was withdrawn. 488 published files that did not build alone were replaced by repaired files, each built alone and run against its proving lane's contract of record first; the assembled library then took 19,414 of 19,632 verified rewrites and left out 218, where it had left out 706. Lifting moved from leaf functions to classes: the seek-cover tasks (11 methods), the motion tree's composer (18) and a spatial-library class (4) are in, each with unsafe code forbidden in its module, and the audio engine's base sound class (9) is tested and waits for a green pipeline. The class lanes read verified rewrites more closely than anything before them and found, in one evening: three header comments that contradict their code, a contract that draws five routes on which the original faults, a contract that covers four of eight child slots, and two more contracts with a zero stack fill hiding an uninitialised read. Two partly proven functions of one to two kilobytes were verified whole by Haiku lanes, each on the first attempt under the new brief, with four and seven wrong versions rejected; three others gained four to thirteen proven stages and stay open. The stack-fill audit stands at 136 settled of 2,081: 106 depend on the zero fill, 29 pass with the pattern as well.The coordinator's faults this hour, in order of weight. It told the owner that the pipeline run measuring the repair had passed; it had read that run's manifest and not its conclusion. The assembled-library job passed and the lift-test job failed, because one older lift test crate supplied a constant that a repaired rewrite now defines for itself. Three lift commits were pushed onto the failing pipeline before the scorecard showed it. The statement is corrected in chat and in the changelog; the crate is fixed after building all 80 lift test crates to find every such collision (it was the only one); the run on the fix is queued, and no tracked code is committed until its conclusion, read as a conclusion, is success. The repair commit also took two commits where one was meant, from a list of paths that assumed one folder. The rule that would have prevented the main fault is now applied: before a change to verified files is committed, every crate that includes verified files is built. On proofs: the coordinator's re-run at 300 trials has now twice held a good claim whose wrong version fails on under one trial in a hundred; held claims of that kind are re-run at the contract's own count before they are treated as holds, and five more are being re-run so now. The three blockers. First, the coordinator's rate of error under its own rate of change, now seven slips in three hours and one of them a false report: fewer changes per hour, each validated before the next, is the correction, and the lanes do not need the coordinator to move this fast. Second, proofs that cover less than they say, where the class lifts have become a second, independent audit. Third, the owner's open decisions: the lane count, and the host-platform experiment. Accelerating against the 24-hour baseline.
01:05An average hour of verified code, a good hour of lifting, the model changed on the owner's instruction, and thirty lanes cut short by the coordinator in making the change. Between 00:04 and 01:03: verified code up by 13,805 bytes in 187 functions (14,039 bytes an hour, against 14,137 over the last 24 hours); 41 routines lifted, to 1,352, in five classes: a move-between-points task, the mirror render phase, the game camera, the follow-point-route task and the front-end's layout frame. The verified set passed 20,000 functions. Luna lanes that ended in the hour verified 214 functions and 13,888 bytes in 28 lane-hours, with 24 claims held. Nothing was withdrawn. A function of two and a half kilobytes, the scene-draw render phase's render method, was verified whole by a Haiku lane: 22 contracts and 8 wrong versions, with the return register listed as not compared after a survey of every call through its virtual slot. At 00:52 the owner said that lanes are Muse lanes from now on. One pilot lane was run first; the launcher, the finishers, the supervisor, the watch and the memory guard were changed to handle lanes of either model, each change checked by the shell's own parser before it replaced the script in use; thirty Muse lanes were running by 01:00. Of the 24 held claims, 19 are false holds: two lanes ran each wrong version for 100 trials beside a proof of 1,000, and the re-run pairs a wrong version with its proof only when the two contracts are otherwise equal. Two more claims of another lane had been held for an out-of-date wrong-version contract left beside a current one; that rule was widened, tested on that lane and on a lane whose holds must stay, applied, and the two recovered.The coordinator's faults this hour. entry.title: Shaft channel steps (spdShaft) lifted from their verified rewrites and proven
entry.summary: From lane l-cls17.
entry.content:
From lane l-cls17.

What was asked

Lift the shaft class of the engine's spatial library, the family named by the executable's type information, from its verified 32-bit rewrites to portable Rust that owns its data. Lift only what is verified, and prove each lifted method against its rewrite.

What the family is

The class has four step methods, all verified: each advances one of four channels by a step length and returns the channel's third direction seed. Each step stores the length, works out three direction seeds from one gain, one of two calibration pairs and a table of twelve floats, mixes the seeds with the table, and clears a pending byte. The seeds are normalised unless a flag byte is set, in which case each channel uses a fixed unit axis. The constructor and the matrix update are unverified and are not lifted. The physical meaning of the step is not established (Unknown).

FactValueStatus
Verified step methods4 of 6 listed methodsVerified: rewrites and their checker contracts
Lifted and proven4 of 4Verified: differential test on the 32-bit target
Steps compared bit for bit160,101 over 20,000 objectsVerified: test run
Deliberate faults caught5 faults, each on all 4 channelsVerified: test run
Unsafe code in the lifted module0 (the rewrites had 52 tokens)Verified: count

What was found

The header comments of the verified rewrites for three of the four channels give the fixed seeds when the flag is set as the unit vector on the first axis. The code, which the checker's contracts compare with the original, uses a different axis for each channel. The contracts exercise that path, so the comments are the error. Verified by reading the rewrites and their contracts.

The square-root helper that every step calls is a callee outside the game-function database. A port must supply a root that matches the original's helper bit for bit. Whether the helper is correctly rounded is not established.

Two of the first mutants were equivalent: swapping the operands of the cross-seed product changes no result, because the two operands carry the same not-a-number. A table product swap is observable, and a probe confirmed that a not-a-number takes its payload from the first operand under this build's code generation.

What was decided

The lifted methods take a host trait for the square-root callee and return the third seed. Each product and sum pins its operand order with a value barrier. Wrong versions are a second writing of the steps with one deliberate fault each, run on every channel; a control writing with no fault must agree with the rewrites before the faults count.

How to reproduce

Run the host tests of the shaft module in the maths crate, then the differential test crate on the 32-bit target with a time limit. The test crate includes the tracked rewrite files by path and needs the game's constants read from the executable's mapped image.

entry.title: Lifting the motion composer: combining filter, data block and sequencing methods
entry.summary: From lane l-cls14.
entry.content:
From lane l-cls14.

What was asked: turn the verified 32-bit rewrites of three classes of the motion tree's optimised composer into portable Rust that owns its data, and prove each lifted method against its rewrite. What is reported: 18 of the 31 verified methods lifted and proven; 13 deferred with reasons; 23 unverified methods of the same classes not touched.

What the family looks like

The combining filter is a poll tree: a child list, one mode word that marks each child as an OR-term or an AND-term, and a fold accumulator that shares the mode word. The optimised data block holds two bulk tables, cleared and rebuilt as a unit. The composer's own methods sequence work: most of them first run the composer's pending-list drain through its own virtual slot, unless immediate mode is on, then step a sequence counter or forward to one numbered callee. The composer's slots for the drain, the gate pass and the node handler are themselves verified methods, so a composition can bind them to the lifted code.

What was lifted and how it is proven

Each class is one owning type. Every call the original makes to code that is not lifted is a method of a trait, so the proof compares every call in order with its arguments, along with the results and every word the rewrite writes. Each proof runs on real 32-bit objects through the shared checker runtime; the tests are seeded and run in under a fifth of a second. Each lifted method has a deliberately wrong copy in the same run, and each is caught. Twenty-seven differential tests and thirty host edge tests pass.

What the proofs found

A rewrite's doc comment gives the wrong return value for the table reset: the code returns a different offset than the comment states. The lift follows the code, which the run confirms, and the comment should be corrected. The poll rewrite reads eight inline child slots, but the checker's contract draws child counts only from zero to four and the negative values, so counts five to eight agree with the rewrite and are not verified against the original.

What is still missing

Thirteen verified methods are not lifted. One returns an address computed from the inner block, and the record family (twelve methods) stores per-opcode node records with payloads taken from argument memory, handler calls through pointers read from that memory, and address arithmetic on arguments. Those need a decision on opaque derived handles and a node-record model per opcode. The four callees of the forwarders and the drain are unverified methods of the same class and need lifting before those forwards can run in a port. Thread-local lookups for the filter owner and the block manager belong behind a thread-context trait in the platform crate.

entry.title: Counted-run search, table reset, flagged stores and record access: 35 instances proven in seven families
entry.summary: From lane l-free27.
entry.content:
From lane l-free27.

Asked. Lift a group of 154 verified small functions that call nothing (27 of 38 bytes, 28 of 39, 24 of 40, 27 of 41, 28 of 42, 20 of 43; 6,221 bytes), by finding the families they belong to and lifting each family once.

Found. The names did not decide the families; the rewrites did. Grouping by what each rewrite reads, writes, returns and branches on gave seven families of four or more members, two of them instances of routines that are already lifted. Most of the rest are singletons or groups of two or three. Five of the 154 cannot be checked, because their rewrites call helpers that no tracked file defines or have no export.

FamilyMembersWhat the routine doesWhere it lives
Counted-run search8Compares a word with each entry of a counted run inside an object, in order, and answers a flag, an index, a masked address or a masked keyNew lifted module counted_run
Sentinel table reset4Clears 128 eight-byte records to an empty marker and a zero half-word, clears an optional flag byte before the run, and returns the endNew lifted module sentinel_table
Flagged pair store4Writes two parameters into two fields of an object, sets or ORs a flag byte between them, and returns a fixed valueNew lifted module flagged_pair_store
Record word read5Reads a record pointer and a validity byte from global tables by index, answers a fixed value for the null index and for a missing record, and otherwise reads one word of the recordNew lifted module record_word_read
Guarded record store and flag read4Stores a byte, a word or a scaled word into a record selected by index, guarded by its validity byte or its pointer; reads one flag byte of a recordNew lifted module record_field_access
Constant initialisers6Writes constants, and the address of a class vtable word, into fixed fields and returns the objectExisting constant_writes, unchanged
Block copies4Copies four words between the object and one caller buffer, in one directionExisting word_block, unchanged

Verified. Each instance was run against its verified rewrite on the 32-bit target with 1,000 generated cases: the returned value and every byte of the memory the rewrite can touch were compared. No instance differed. Every deliberately wrong version of every family (a wrong offset, a wrong stride or count, a wrong constant, a wrong answer form or null answer, a missing or extra store, a flipped guard, a wrong return) was caught on every instance: 123 wrong-version runs in all. The host edge tests pass on the 64-bit host, and the workspace check passes there too.

Decided. Families under four members are listed and left, as the brief says. The streaming record accessors share one global table and one null index: nine routines in all. They split by shape into a read family of five and a store family of four, and both are proven here. The float clamp-and-store routines (three members, one global maximum), the slot-state byte tests (three), and the bit-field readers (three) are listed with their shapes.

Process finding. A wrong version that differs only at one fixed position of a run is caught only when the generated inputs place the single equal word there. The first run of the search family missed a run shifted by one word on one instance, with 1,000 cases and random words. Generating one case in four with exactly one equal entry, at the first, the last or a random place, made every wrong version caught.

Process finding. A wrong version that changes a guard can write through a pointer the original never writes through. The generated states must follow the original's guard, not the wrong version under test, or the rewrite itself faults on the test's memory. Separately, a rewrite that calls a helper no tracked file defines is not counted: three word-copy routines of the audio meters use such helpers and are listed as missing.

Process finding. An instance of a family that is already lifted is the cheapest proof: the existing routine is unchanged and only the instance table and a test crate are new. Two of the seven families were proven this way (constant initialisers, word-block copies).

entry.title: Sixteen verified rewrites withdrawn in a day and all sixteen proven again: what the causes were, and what a proof with ordinary inputs cannot see
entry.summary: This closes the account opened in the entry "Widening a proof's inputs" earlier today, which stood at seven. Over the day sixteen rewrites that had passed their proofs were shown to differ from the original, were withdrawn, had their causes located, and were proven again on contracts that would have caught the fault. Not one of the sixteen was caught by its contract of record: in every case where it was tried, the contract of record passes the faulty form as well.
entry.content:
This closes the account opened in the entry "Widening a proof's inputs" earlier today, which stood at seven. Over the day sixteen rewrites that had passed their proofs were shown to differ from the original, were withdrawn, had their causes located, and were proven again on contracts that would have caught the fault. Not one of the sixteen was caught by its contract of record: in every case where it was tried, the contract of record passes the faulty form as well.

What was asked

If a proof is a thousand random trials inside the ranges its contract declares, what kinds of fault survive it, how are they found, and what does it take to prove the corrected form properly?

The causes

CauseRewritesWhy ordinary trials passed
A float converted to an integer with a cast, where the original's instruction gives a fixed result for not-a-number and for values that do not fitEight, as the first or a later faultContracts draw small floats. The two forms agree everywhere but at the ends of the range and for not-a-number.
A float comparison written with the neighbouring predicate: "not less than" for the original's "not less than or equal"FourThe two differ only when the operands are equal, and random floats are never equal. In one of the four the code was also unreachable under its contract.
An integer comparison with the wrong signednessTwoThe values drawn never had the top bit set.
A read taken from the wrong place on the stack: the neighbouring frame slot, two slots merged into one, a key read from the caller's row where the original reloads the table'sTwoThe contract filled the two places with the same value, or with zero.
A read made earlier than the original makes it, or once where the original repeats itOne, twice overNo trial put a null where the early read would fault, and no callee changed the table between the repeated reads.
Two arguments of a call in the wrong orderOneThe contract's inputs made the two interchangeable.
A float sum whose operand order was not pinnedOneThe order shows only in the payload of the result when both operands are not-a-number.
Logic: an early return that skips a final check, a missing test of a flag bit, a missing branch, AND where the original has OR, an index that the original wrapsFour, with five such faults between them, each behind another faultThe inputs never took the path: an empty range with a negative limit, a flag bit never set, an index never negative.
A constant written into the rewrite where the original loads it from the imageOneThe contract never varied the image's value.

The counts add to more than sixteen because most rewrites had more than one fault. At least eight of the sixteen showed a second, third or fourth fault only after the first was corrected and every input was widened; one had four that all had to be corrected before any widened run passed.

What was learned about proofs

  • A proof covers the inputs its contract draws and the memory its contract compares, and nothing else. Three further gaps of that kind were measured the same day, apart from input ranges: 54 contracts of record set a value at an address inside the code section, where the function never reads it; 148 leave a write to data uncompared; 2,081 set the stack fill to zero, and in a sample of forty about one in six of those proofs depends on the zero in what the function stores.
  • Reading is not enough to withdraw, and not enough to clear. An audit read the original's instruction behind three float comparisons and found the predicate wrong in each. One was then shown on the checker and withdrawn; one was shown once its contract's addresses were corrected; the third has the wrong predicate and no observable difference, because what the comparison selects is added to a zero, and it stayed verified. Nothing was withdrawn on a reading alone, and for one of the three that restraint was right.
  • A widened contract can itself be wrong. Two rewrites that failed widened contracts were cleared: in one the contract widened a word in memory without the scripted callee answer that holds the same word, and in the other the only failing trials were ones on which the original itself faults.
  • Three functions read a frame word they never wrote. For two the proof now holds only for a zero in that word and says so as its first narrowing; for the third the original turned out to overwrite the word before any read, which the lane established from the instructions.
  • The method that located the hardest case, four faults in one function's use of its stack, was a map: every access through the stack pointer resolved to its real frame slot, accounting for pushes and for callees that clean their own arguments, set side by side with the rewrite's variables. The script takes any function.

What was decided

  • Withdraw on a difference shown on the stock checker on trials the original completes, the same hour; prove again only with every input the function reads widened, the special values counted on completed trials with an instrumented copy, and the withdrawn form run as a wrong version that must fail.
  • The production brief carries the rules as versions b27 and b28: predicates and signedness from the original's instruction, arguments against the pushes, operand order pinned, memory read where and as often as the original reads it, values loaded from the image, addresses checked against the function's own operands, no zero stack fill to make a proof pass, and what a contract must reach to see each.
  • The checker's driver refuses a contract that sets a value in code. The audits of the three measured gaps continue as unattended runs; each ends in a list to withdraw and a list of contracts to strengthen.

How to reproduce it

Each rewrite's strengthening lane left, beside its corrected rewrite: the contract of record, the widened contract, a contract per wrong version identical to its partner but for the library, the verdicts, and the counts of special values that reached the corrected code on completed trials. The coordinator ran each set again on the stock checker before importing it. The changelog entries titled "Rewrites: … withdrawn" give each withdrawal's evidence, and the entries "… more functions pass the checker" that follow them give the re-imports.
