Unsafe in lifted code0The rewrites they replace hold 107 uses of unsafe across 50 files
Not reached128Families below four members, singletons and routines not reduced to a shared shape

Decided. The lifted routines live in new modules of the core crate, one line each in its module list, and nothing else in the crate changes. Each family's test crate includes the tracked rewrite files by path and runs the lifted routine against them on the 32-bit target. The host build of each test crate checks, and the lifted modules carry their own unit tests on the 64-bit host. None of the lifted routines computes with a float. Two broadcast rewrites copy a float through a single-precision load and store; the lift copies the bits, and the test compares them bit for bit on generated patterns, including not-a-number patterns, and they agree. The float helpers that four copy rewrites declare are never called on their path.

How to reproduce. Group the verified rewrites with the number-masked form, then read the role of each rewrite; the family tables and their parameters are in the lane's generator scripts. Build a test crate with the 32-bit target and run it. The differential harness runs each instance on a fresh generated state, compares every word the rewrite may write, and checks that the rewrite's result matches the lifted result.

Confidence. Verified for the seven families on this lane's runs. Inferred for the claim that the families cover the shapes in the group: the 130 others were not checked one by one against a shared shape. The parameters of the block-copy family were transcribed by reading each rewrite; the tests would show a wrong transcription, and none was found.

entry.title: Small free functions: 83 instances in five families proven against lifted routines
entry.summary: From lane l-free22.
entry.content:
From lane l-free22.

Asked. Lift a group of 155 verified free functions of 13, 15 and 17 bytes that call nothing, by finding the routines they are instances of and proving each instance against one lifted routine.

Found. Five families hold 83 of the 155: a store of one parameter into a field at a constant offset (50 instances, byte or word, four kinds of return), a copy of one static word into another (11), a comparison of a word with a constant or the parameter (6), a routine that writes constants into a few fields and returns zero, one or the object (10), and a read of a byte or word at a base plus an index times a stride (6). The other 72 are listed in groups, with the reason each is not lifted. Five of the field-store rewrites call a helper that no tracked file defines.

FactValueMeaning
Field-store instances50Byte (24) and word (26) stores; return zero, the parameter, the parameter's low byte, or nothing
Word-copy instances11One word read and one word written, return zero; fifteen static words in all
Word-test instances6Equal, not equal and signed greater, against a constant or the parameter; two read from static words
Constant-write instances10One to three constant writes of one to four bytes; return zero, one or the object
Indexed-read instances6Byte or word read at base plus index times stride, 32-bit wrapping arithmetic
Missing, does not compile5Rewrites that call a helper named wrf; no tracked file or checker runtime defines it
Lifted code addedfive modules in lf-coreNo unsafe code and no addresses; each family is one method on a small owning type with a table of instances
Proof1,000 cases per instanceResult and every byte or word the rewrite may touch compared after each call; floats compared as bits
Wrong versionsfour per family, 64 cases eachCaught by every instance in every family

Verified. In the final pass all five 32-bit test crates pass their three tests each (the differential comparison, the wrong versions, and the instance-table check); the host tests of lf-core and of the five test crates pass, and the host check of the lane's workspace passes.

Finding: the float return quiets a signalling NaN. One float-returning rewrite in the indexed-read family returned a different bit pattern from the lifted word when the entry was a signalling not-a-number: the rewrite's return passes through the floating-point return register, which sets the quiet bit. The lifted read now models that return (a float result is quieted in the same way), and the test plants signalling and quiet not-a-number patterns in each word entry. The original routine is expected to behave the same way because it returns through the same register; this is inferred from the convention, not read from the original.

Finding: five verified rewrites do not compile from the repository. The audio parameter-store rewrites call a helper named wrf. The checker index records them as verified, but no tracked file and no checker runtime defines the helper, so the test crate fails to build on them. They are listed as missing and were not worked around.

Decided. A routine whose whole content is one address behind a null check (nine rewrites) is listed, not lifted. A family of fewer than four members is listed. A read-modify-write of flag bits is listed. Every lifted method takes its object as bytes or a table, so no lifted code depends on pointer width. The tests keep indexes small enough that every read stays inside the test object; the wrap-around of the offset arithmetic is covered by host tests of the lifted method.

Process finding. Two runtime tests that share global slots raced when they ran in parallel and failed one run in several; one lock per test program fixes it. A test that compares a predicate on a random word almost never reaches the equal case: the test draws the tested word around the constant instead.

Still open. The 72 listed functions are groups, not lifts. The five wrf rewrites need the helper defined by the repository, or the rewrites changed, before they can be proven. The field-store lift is one method over a table, a weak lift: the proof shows the table describes the rewrites, not that the family's meaning is understood.

entry.title: A host for the finished game: what Bevy offers, what this engine needs, and why the renderer should be written against wgpu first
entry.summary: The owner asked, ahead of time, whether the Bevy engine should be the platform under the game once its logic exists as portable Rust, so that it can be built for many targets. Two research lanes ran side by side: one read Bevy's current state from primary sources, one measured what this engine needs from a host out of what the project already knows. This entry is the coordinator's synthesis. Nothing was installed or built for it, and the plan is unchanged until the owner decides.
entry.content:
The owner asked, ahead of time, whether the Bevy engine should be the platform under the game once its logic exists as portable Rust, so that it can be built for many targets. Two research lanes ran side by side: one read Bevy's current state from primary sources, one measured what this engine needs from a host out of what the project already knows. This entry is the coordinator's synthesis. Nothing was installed or built for it, and the plan is unchanged until the owner decides.

What was asked

Is Bevy the right host for a game that is not being designed around an entity-component system, but reproduced exactly from an existing engine with its own loop, renderer, mixer and streaming? Two uses were kept apart throughout: (A) Bevy as a platform layer only, with the game's own simulation running inside it; (B) a real port onto Bevy's entity-component system, renderer features, animation and physics.

What this engine needs from a host

AreaFindingLabel
Shaders969 distinct shader programs, all Direct3D 9 shader model 3.0. The project's own translator turns 965 of them into SPIR-V that passes its structural validator; the four that fail share one cause, an input semantic with no slot in the binding convention.Verified: the translator's test over the owner's installed files, run for this entry.
RendererA deferred pipeline: a four-target geometry buffer, stencil-masked lights, cascade and cube shadows, a high-dynamic-range post chain. Draw lists are recorded on worker threads and replayed by one render thread. Textures are block-compressed in three formats plus two uncompressed ones.Verified from earlier surveys; the draw-list structure is Likely.
AudioThe game mixes its own sound. A host has to pull samples through a callback and little else.Verified.
Threads and timeExact wait semantics for its synchronisation, a millisecond clock with its wrap behaviour, and a simulation step that follows the original's arithmetic on frame time.Verified for the calls; Likely for the step.
FilesAsynchronous, prioritised, cancellable byte-range reads into large archives, read at run time from the player's own installed copy.Verified.
Code that is not being rewrittenA compression library, an image codec and a collision library have replacements. The ragdoll behaviour middleware has no open replacement and would need a clean-room reimplementation.Verified from the library inventory.
The frame itselfThe main loop, the update order, the hand-off of draw data to the render thread and the creation of the window are in the part of the code that is encrypted on disk, which the inventory does not cover.Unknown. This is the largest gap for any host.

What Bevy offers today

QuestionFindingLabel and source
Current stateVersion 0.20 was released on 8 October 2026, on version 30 of the wgpu graphics library. Releases come every three to four months with breaking changes and migration guides; no 1.0 and no stability commitment is announced.Verified: the project's news page and release process page; the release dates were checked a second time by the coordinator.
A custom renderer inside itAn application can draw its own vertex and index buffers with its own pipeline, with none of Bevy's meshes, materials or lights; an example in the repository at the 0.20 tag shows it. The renderer can also be switched off with the window and the loop kept, and an application can own the loop. Whether an application can create its own graphics surface from Bevy's window is shown by no example.Verified from the repository's examples; the last point Unknown.
Shader inputBevy's own shader language is WGSL; support for GLSL was removed in 0.20. It accepts SPIR-V and translates it through the naga library, whose output for Metal and Direct3D 12 is a primary target and for WebGL and WebGPU a secondary one.Verified from the 0.20 documentation and migration guide.
Reading the game's dataA custom asset source is supported, with an asynchronous, seekable reader. The documented contract of a read is a whole file; ranged reads into a multi-gigabyte container during play are not documented either way.Verified from the documentation; the fit is Unknown until tested.
PlatformsDesktop Linux, macOS, iOS and Android are listed as supported by the project's own example tester; Windows on Direct3D 12 and the web are listed as in progress. The project's continuous integration has no Windows target for ARM64 processors. The one report for that platform is an open rendering fault on a Qualcomm integrated graphics processor under Vulkan, opened in June 2026, with no maintainer reply. No console support is documented.Verified: the example tester page and the issue, which the coordinator also read.
PrecedentsThe closest found is a rewrite of an older shooter's engine on Bevy, whose author kept the world and client state in one central structure and wrote most of the rendering by hand against wgpu. No reimplementation of an older open-world game on Bevy or on wgpu in Rust was found.Verified from that project's own description; the absence is as far as two searches went.
AlternativesThe windowing library and wgpu that Bevy itself is built on can be used directly with the project's own loop. SDL 3 reaches consoles, but only through ports under a non-disclosure agreement. Fyrox reached 1.0 in September 2026. Godot can host Rust through bindings, with consoles through a commercial third party.Verified for versions and dates; the console terms from the projects' own pages.

The coordinator's reading

This part is judgement, not finding.

  • Use (B), a port onto Bevy's entity-component system and its own renderer, animation and physics, has no case here. The project's rule is exact reproduction of the original's behaviour, and each of those subsystems would replace something that is being reproduced. The one precedent found made the same choice for the same reason.
  • Use (A), Bevy as a platform layer, is feasible: its custom-pass route, its acceptance of SPIR-V and its optional renderer cover what the engine needs. What it costs is exposure to a renderer interface that changed in each of the last two releases, a platform (Windows on ARM64, which is the owner's own machine) that the project does not test, and no route to consoles.
  • The renderer should be written against wgpu directly, as a crate of its own, and not against Bevy's rendering interface. Bevy is built on the same library, so the same passes would run inside a Bevy application or inside a bare window-and-loop shell, and the choice of shell stays reversible behind the platform traits the lifted crates already use. The translated shaders enter the same way in both.
  • Web and mobile are limited less by the host than by the data: the game's files must come from the player's own copy, which on the web means a file the player selects, and the block-compressed textures are not usable as they are on most mobile graphics processors.

What was decided

Nothing yet beyond recording this. Two questions are with the owner: whether a lane may fetch the Bevy and wgpu crates for an experiment kept outside the main workspace (the project's rule is that nothing is downloaded without his approval), and whether a host-platform phase goes into the plan.

The experiment proposed, with its pass criteria stated in advance: one section of the map, parsed by the project's own loaders, drawn with one translated shader through passes written against wgpu, once inside a Bevy 0.20 application and once in a bare shell, on the owner's ARM64 Windows machine and on an x86-64 one. It passes if the draw is correct on both machines, the shaders compile on Direct3D 12 and on Vulkan, and the archive is read by ranges without copying the container.

How to reproduce it

The shader figure comes from the translator crate's test over real files, which runs when the game folder's location is given in the environment and is skipped otherwise; it reads the shader containers and writes nothing. The engine's requirements are queries over the project's evidence database and the earlier devlog entries on the executable, the formats and the shaders. The Bevy findings each carry their source in the research lane's report, one hundred sources in all, of which this entry links the two the coordinator read again.

entry.title: A contract that set its globals in the wrong place, and how many others may have
entry.summary: A lane that was sent to make the checker observe one float comparison could not, and reported that the checker was not applying two values its contract set. The checker was applying them exactly where the contract said. The contract said the wrong place.
entry.content:
A lane that was sent to make the checker observe one float comparison could not, and reported that the checker was not applying two values its contract set. The checker was applying them exactly where the contract said. The contract said the wrong place.

What was asked

Why do two globals that a proof's contract sets, a divisor and a size, read back as minus one on both sides whatever value the contract gives them? And if a contract can be wrong in this way without anything noticing, how many are?

What was found

FactValueWhat it means
Where the contract of record puts the two valuesAt addresses a fixed amount below the globals the function reads, inside the code section. Verified.An arithmetic slip when the lane turned an address in the image into an offset from the image base. The worker writes the values there; the function never reads them; both sides read the file's own value of the real globals, which is minus one.
What the proof of record then coveredA grid whose index never leaves zero. It passes 1,000 of 1,000 trials. Verified by reproducing it with an instrumented copy.The proof is real and says much less than it appears to: the part of the function that divides, rounds and indexes was never exercised with a usable divisor.
The same contract with the two addresses correctedThe verified rewrite fails 30 of 1,000 trials; with a positive divisor and size, 85 of 1,000. A copy with one float comparison corrected passes. Verified on the stock worker with an unchanged copy of the driver; the lane wrote its predictions down before running.The rewrite was wrong: a rounding helper compares with "not less than" where the original's instruction is "not less than or equal", which differ for whole-number inputs. An audit had read that from the instruction earlier in the day and could not show it. The rewrite had already been withdrawn on the ground that its proof did not reach the code in doubt; that is now a shown difference.
A deliberately wrong version on the corrected contractFails 494 of 1,000. Verified.The corrected contract sees the code. Under the contract of record a wrong version of that code would have passed.
Contracts of record scanned for the condition16,381 read; 238 functions have no contract file where the index says and were not scanned.The scan follows each verified function to its proving lane's contract; it does not search.
Contracts that place a value or a range in code54 functions.Certain faults in the contract: nothing is ever meant to be set there. Each of those proofs is narrower than it says. Whether the rewrite is right on the wider input is not yet known for any of them.
Contracts that set words the function's body never refers to738 functions, 5,674 words.Some are slips of the same kind, some are values meant for a callee, some are an image address written where an offset is wanted. Not yet separated.
Functions that write to data the contract neither declares nor compares in full148.A rewrite could write something different there and no check would see it.
Functions with the same signature as the one that started this288. In a sample of ten read by hand, nine of the values gate a branch, index a table, feed arithmetic or reach an unchecked output; one is harmless. Inferred from reading listings.The condition usually matters where it occurs.

Correction to an earlier statement

The lane that first met this wrote that the checker does not apply a contract's values at those two addresses. That was wrong, and the changelog entry of the withdrawal repeated the doubt. The checker writes a value where the contract names it and checks nothing about whether that is a place the function reads. That is the gap: not a fault in what the checker does, but something it never looked at.

What was decided

  • The rewrite stays withdrawn and a strengthening lane is proving the corrected copy, with every other address in its contract checked the same way.
  • The investigation lane continues from counting to measuring: for the 54 certain cases first, then the 148, it corrects the contract and runs the verified rewrite through it on the stock checker. A rewrite that then fails on trials the original completes is withdrawn; one that still passes gets the corrected contract as its contract of record.
  • The lane wrote a check for the driver that refuses a contract which places a value outside writable data, with tests. It will be adopted in a narrower form: a refusal for code, gaps and addresses outside the image, which can never be meant; a warning for read-only data, because varying a constant the original loads from there is a legitimate test and one the day's other findings call for; and a verdict file that records the refusal.
  • The production brief will tell lanes how to turn an image address into the offset a contract wants, to check that every address they set is one the function's body refers to, and to confirm with a deliberately wrong version that each value they set is seen.

How to reproduce it

For a contract, take every address it sets or declares and find the section of the image it falls in; then decode the function and list the absolute data addresses its instructions refer to. An address the contract sets that is in code, or that no instruction of the function refers to, is a candidate. The lane's script does this for one contract or for the whole verified set and writes the list.

entry.title: Head-swap and constant-store families: 170 instances proven against two lifted methods
entry.summary: From lane l-free21.
entry.content:
From lane l-free21.

Asked. Lift a group of 198 verified 21-byte functions that call nothing, by finding the data they share and lifting each shape once.

Found. Most of the group is one routine: read a global list head, store the old value into a second word, point the head at a static node, and return the old value. One hundred and sixty-two rewrites have this shape. Eight more write two constants into two global words and return zero or nothing. The other 28 members are different shapes (branching readers, bit tests on a record, clears and copies through a record pointer) and are listed, not lifted.

FactValueMeaning
Head-swap members162Verified rewrites with one head read, one save write, one head write to a node, and a return of the read value
Textual groups11 for the same routineA hash of the normalised text splits one routine into eleven groups; extracting the roles of each rewrite groups them correctly
Constant-store members8Two constants written to two global words, returns zero (seven) or nothing (one)
Lifted code addedtwo methods in one new moduleOne list-head method and one two-word store, with no unsafe code and no addresses
Proof170 instances, 1,000 cases eachEvery returned value and every word compared, rebuilt through the same addresses
Wrong versionshead left unchanged; save takes the node; a store left outCaught for every instance

Verified. The four test crates pass on the 32-bit target (59, 59, 47 and 9 tests, none failing). The 64-bit workspace check and the host edge tests pass.

Decided. Prove the list family as one method on a table of link words, with words named by index, rather than as a class. The store-order version of the list routine is equivalent on every input the instances can reach, because the save word and the head are always different words. It is asserted to agree, and it is not counted as a caught wrong version.

Process finding. A differential test shows a wrong version is caught only if it can differ on a reachable input. Any order-only mutant over distinct words is equivalent, so the next brief should name that case instead of requiring a catch.

Still open. The 28 odd members need separate lifts with their own proofs. The return value of the constant-store family is checked by the test, not carried by the lifted method.

entry.title: Quotient-store family: 229 more instances proven against one lifted routine
entry.summary: From lane l-free20.
entry.content:
From lane l-free20.

Asked. Lift a group of 265 verified 25-byte functions that call nothing, by finding the data they share and lifting each instance family once.

Found. Most of the group is one routine: read two single-precision globals, divide, and store the quotient in a third global. Two hundred and twenty-nine rewrites have this shape. Their return is absent, a dead integer zero, or the stored quotient. The other 36 members are different shapes (branching accessors, pointer-arithmetic setters, store-only copies) and are listed, not lifted.

FactValueMeaning
Members of the routine229Verified rewrites with one division, two global reads, one global write
Return kinds125 none, 85 dead zero, 19 quotientThe dead return is checked to be zero and not compared further
Lifted code addednoneThe existing quotient routine in the vehicle module is proven for each instance
Proof229 instances, 1,000 cases eachEvery effect compared bit for bit, including sources and not-a-number payloads
Wrong versionsoperands swapped, wrong destinationBoth caught for every instance

Verified. All four test crates pass on the 32-bit target. A deliberately swapped lift fails 58 of 58 instances in one batch. The 64-bit host edge tests (7) pass.

Decided. Prove the instances against the existing routine rather than write a second copy. Batches are at most 58 rewrites per test crate. Non-vehicle instances are tested against the vehicle module for now; a move to a neutral module is a coordinator decision.

Process finding. A copy of a tracked source into a build tree keeps its old modification time, and cargo then reuses a stale binary. The generator now gives copies a new time. Any future generator that copies sources must do the same.

Still open. Six flag-gated field setters depend on a shared record lookup that is not a verified function. They wait until that lookup is verified.

entry.title: One red pipeline run, three causes, and a fourth thing it uncovered: 706 verified rewrites whose published file is not the code that was proven
entry.summary: The pipeline on the public repository failed on an afternoon commit after passing all morning. The failing jobs had three unrelated causes, two of them faults in the project's own tooling, and following the third to its end showed that 3.7% of the verified rewrites cannot be built into the assembled library from the file that is published for them.
entry.content:
The pipeline on the public repository failed on an afternoon commit after passing all morning. The failing jobs had three unrelated causes, two of them faults in the project's own tooling, and following the third to its end showed that 3.7% of the verified rewrites cannot be built into the assembled library from the file that is published for them.

What was asked

Why did a commit that only added three lifted routines break the job that assembles every verified rewrite into one library, and the job that checks the rewrite tree against its index?

What was found

FactValueWhat it means
Index rows lostFive verified rewrites had a file and no row in the index. Verified.Three finishers and the coordinator ran the importer at the same moment. Each read the index, added its rows and wrote the whole file back; the last writer's copy dropped the others' rows. The fault was on the safe side, verified work not counted, and the consistency check caught it within the hour.
Files the assembler dropped on the failing commit35 in one shard, of which 5 were at fault. Verified by replaying the shard locally.When a shard fails to build, the assembler reads the compiler's messages and drops the rewrites they point at. It took any position in a file named lib.rs to be in the shard's own root file. The checker runtime's export macro lives in a file of the same name, so an error reached through the macro was looked up by line number in the wrong file and blamed on a rewrite that compiles. Each round dropped another innocent file, the two that really failed were never dropped, and after 30 rounds the job gave up.
Had the assembler done this before?Unknown. The earlier manifests are not kept.Earlier passing runs may have left out rewrites that compile. It cost nothing but their place in the library, and the next run includes them.
Verified rewrites left out of the assembled library, with the assembler corrected706 of 19,026. Verified from the manifest of the first passing run.472 do not compile on their own and 234 are refused before compiling. This is the finding that matters.
Why the 472 do not compile248 call a function that is not in the file, 72 use a constant and 64 a type that is not there, 13 import something that does not exist, 18 use a reserved word as a name, 13 have an unclosed bracket, 7 define a name twice, 3 define a second panic handler.A lane proves a function with a library built from its own crate, where helpers, constants and types may sit in a shared module. Only the one file is published. In two cases the published file is a three-line wrapper and the whole body stayed in the lane's folder.
Why the 234 are refused206 use a runtime of the lane's own in place of the shared one, 17 have no export the assembler recognises, 5 still carry a wrong version beside the right one.Mostly early lanes, from before the shared runtime was the rule.
When they were proven346 on the second checker version, 213 recorded on the current one.128 of the 213 are old files whose proofs the regression lanes have re-run; 85 come from production and queue lanes working on the current checker. It is still happening, slowly.

What this does and does not say

It does not say these 706 rewrites are wrong. Each passed its trials, with its wrong version rejected where the checker version required one, as a library built by its lane. What it says is narrower and still serious: for these functions the file in the repository is not the thing the checker ran. The coordinator's independent re-run has the same blind spot, because it runs the lane's built library and never builds the published file. A reader who takes the published file as the verified code is, for 3.7% of the set, reading something that does not build.

What was decided

  • The importer and the withdrawal script now hold one lock from reading the index to writing it. The five rows are restored.
  • The assembler counts an error position only when it is in the shard's own root file or the shard's own copy of a rewrite, with three tests. On the failing commit it then drops exactly the files that do not compile and builds in two rounds. The pipeline passes again.
  • The 706 stay counted as verified for now, with this entry as the statement of what that count includes. A tool lane is classifying them by what a repair takes, writing a check the importer can run on every file before it is published (does it compile alone, against the shared runtime, as the assembler would place it), repairing two of each class from the proving lane's own source and proving each repaired file by building it alone and running the contract of record against that build. What a script can repair is repaired by script; the rest goes to lanes; what cannot be made whole is proven again.
  • Once that check exists, a published file that does not compile on its own is held at import with the reason, and the production brief says so.

How to reproduce it

The assembled library's manifest is an artifact of every pipeline run: its excluded list has one record per file left out, with the stage and the compiler's first message. Grouping that list by message gives the table above. The assembler's fault is covered by the tests added with the correction: an error reached through the runtime's macro is attributed to the rewrite it came from and not to the rewrite that owns the same line number in the shard.

Update, the same evening: 706 down to 218

The tool lane classified the 706, repaired by script what a script could repair from the proving lanes' own source, and wrote a prover that needs no model: it builds each repaired file alone and runs the proving lane's contract of record against that build on the stock checker, with the lane's wrong version where one exists. Of 550 repaired files it settled, 501 pass: 130 with their wrong version rejected, 371 where the proving lane has no wrong version that can still be run. 488 of them replaced their published files in two commits, after the coordinator checked each file's hash against the prover's record and that the set builds alone. The next pipeline run assembled 19,414 of 19,632 verified rewrites and left out 218, where the run before the repair left out 706 of 19,593. Verified.

The importer now runs the same build-alone check on every claim before it is published, and a claim whose file fails is held with the compiler's reason. What remains of the 218: files that call a helper or use a type no script could trace to a definition, 18 that use a word the current language edition reserves, 9 on a lane runtime whose repair is not a pure renaming, and 8 with no export the assembler recognises. They go to lanes.

entry.title: Widening a proof's inputs: seven verified rewrites differed from the original, and only four were the fault being looked for
entry.summary: An audit that began with one question, how verified rewrites convert floats to integers, ended the day as a general test: take a verified rewrite and its contract of record, widen the contract so that every float the function can read takes extreme values on a share of trials, and run it again on the stock checker. Seven rewrites that had passed their proofs differ from the original under that test, on trials the original completes. All seven were withdrawn; five are already proven again with the cause corrected or are with a lane for it.
entry.content:
An audit that began with one question, how verified rewrites convert floats to integers, ended the day as a general test: take a verified rewrite and its contract of record, widen the contract so that every float the function can read takes extreme values on a share of trials, and run it again on the stock checker. Seven rewrites that had passed their proofs differ from the original under that test, on trials the original completes. All seven were withdrawn; five are already proven again with the cause corrected or are with a lane for it.

What was asked

A proof here is thousands of random trials inside the ranges its contract declares. What does a proof with ordinary ranges fail to see?

What was found

What differedFunctionsStatus
A float converted to a 32-bit integer with Rust's cast, where the original's truncating instruction gives a fixed result for not-a-number and for values that do not fit.Two.Verified on the stock checker. Both corrected and proven again with widened contracts, the old form failing as the wrong version.
A float converted through a 64-bit integer store whose low half is used: the two sides differ for positive infinity and beyond the 64-bit limit.Two, one from a single and one from a double.Verified. One corrected and proven again; the other has a corrected copy that passes and is with a strengthening lane.
A clamp the original does with a signed comparison and the rewrite did unsigned: they differ when the value has its top bit set.One.Verified: the original's conditional instruction was read and a one-line change passes both contracts. With a strengthening lane.
The final sign of one value in a bank of floats.One.The difference is verified on a trial both sides complete; the cause is not located. With an investigation lane.
An argument to a later call, when an earlier callee answers a float of large magnitude.One.The difference is verified; the cause is not located. The checker's report shows only the first few calls of a trial, which hides the call that differs.

Scale, as far as it is known. Of 15,700 verified rewrites, 291 contain a float-to-integer cast. In 193 of those every cast is guarded exactly as the instruction behaves, which is safe by construction: the audit computed both forms over the special values and a million random bit patterns, and no unguarded form agrees with the instruction on positive overflow, whatever is done with the result. Of the 95 that needed the test, 56 have been tested; in 28 the test passed without an extreme value reaching the conversion, which settles nothing; 39 are being tested now. A further 66 files convert through a 64-bit integer with no guard at the limit and are candidates. Nothing comparable has been counted yet for signed and unsigned comparisons.

Why the proofs of record passed

None of them was wrong about what it tested. Their contracts drew small, ordinary values, so a conversion never met a value that did not fit and a sum never had its top bit set. The first lane to look at this took a passing run for a blind spot in the checker; it was the inputs.

What was decided

  • A rewrite known to differ from the original on an input the original handles is withdrawn, whether or not the game is known to produce that input. In every case here that is unknown.
  • Briefs carry two rules. A float is never converted with a bare cast unless the code bounds it first as the original does; otherwise the conversion is written to match the instruction, and the function's contract must reach the special values with the bare cast as a wrong version that fails. A comparison or clamp on an integer takes its signedness from the original's conditional instruction, read from the original.
  • The widened test becomes a standing tool, not a one-off: after the conversions, the same run over rewrites that compare integers near their limits.
  • A pass counts for this test only when the extreme values are shown to have reached the code in question, by counting them in an instrumented copy.

How to reproduce

The audit lanes' folders hold the detector for casts, the classifier, the tool that widens a contract and runs it, the widened contracts, the corrected rewrites and the conversion functions with bit-level references and tests.

entry.title: How many lanes this machine can run: measured at thirty, sixty and over a hundred
entry.summary: The machine has 18 logical processors and 48 GB of memory. For most of the project the lane count was set by memory, because a lane's agent process is small and memory was what ran out first in the early weeks. On 10 and 11 October the count was taken to sixty and then to over a hundred, and the result was measured each time. Memory is not the limit for lanes that verify; the processor is.
entry.content:
The machine has 18 logical processors and 48 GB of memory. For most of the project the lane count was set by memory, because a lane's agent process is small and memory was what ran out first in the early weeks. On 10 and 11 October the count was taken to sixty and then to over a hundred, and the result was measured each time. Memory is not the limit for lanes that verify; the processor is.

What was asked

The owner asked for lanes to fill memory down to a 2 GB reserve, first to finish naming and then to keep verification moving, and later asked directly whether adding more agents speeds verification up.

What was found

Lanes of the main modelNewly verified codePer lane-hourWhat else was seen
About 12 (earlier in the week)Not measured by the hour thenAbout 4,000 bytesMemory to spare, processor not saturated.
30 (four hours of the night of 10 to 11 October)25,000 to 51,000 bytes an hour; 129 to 403 functions1,000 to 2,300 bytesProcessor at 100%, 8 to 10 GB of memory unused, small-function lanes finishing most of their batches.
About 60 (two hours the same night)About 19,000 bytes an hour400 to 500 bytesThe coordinator's own commands took up to ten minutes; lanes deferred functions for time.
90 to 115 (the afternoon of 11 October)About 19,000 bytes an hour over two hours, most of it imported after the count had fallen359 bytes181 to 244 threads waiting for 18 processors. Lanes' checker runs hit their time limits. The supervisor took fifteen minutes between imports. The regression runner needed 290 seconds a proof against 13 on a free machine. One coordinator command did not start for 23 minutes. Memory at the reserve, with the floor guard stopping lanes' link steps.

All figures are verified from the hourly scorecards and the system's own counters. The comparison across rows is not perfectly clean: the lanes of the last row included many that had sat through a standby, and batches differ in difficulty. The direction is the same in every measurement.

Why naming is different

A naming lane is one agent reading code, with no compiler and no checker. Forty of them at once named 1,164 functions in two and a half hours, and filling memory with them worked. A verification lane compiles Rust and runs the original and the rewrite thousands of times in checker workers; three such workers per lane, across a hundred lanes, is several times what 18 processors can serve.

What was decided

  • The lane count for verification is the owner's decision and the figures above were put to him with a recommendation of about thirty. Until he answers, the count is held at thirty, which both of the options before him include.
  • Whatever the count, these now hold: lanes of the main model and the regression runner run below normal priority; the coordinator's supervising and importing processes run above normal; lane starts pause when available memory is under 4.5 GB and resume at 6 GB, so that lanes already running do not push the machine under the reserve; a second and, in a wave, a third finisher import ended lanes.
  • Naming lanes and Haiku lanes are counted apart from the thirty: the first are light, and the second are few.

What it cost to find out

About four hours of reduced output across the two days, and lanes whose batches came back a quarter done. Nothing false was recorded: a lane that runs out of time defers, and a re-run that times out imports nothing.

entry.title: Lift: task record sub-object tables and the aim blend (ped_task group, two shapes)
entry.summary: Asked. Lift the 90 verified routines of the ped task group, grouped by the data they share, one shape at a time, each lifted routine proven against its verified 32-bit rewrite.
entry.content:
Asked. Lift the 90 verified routines of the ped task group, grouped by the data they share, one shape at a time, each lifted routine proven against its verified 32-bit rewrite.

Found (Verified). The name group holds about nineteen data shapes. Most shapes have one routine. Two shapes had clear data and were lifted: the four sub-object tables of the task record (two routines that walk them), and the aim blend of the record (one routine with two gate calls and a hook on the target).

ShapeRoutines liftedProofNarrowed
Task record sub-object tables (frame remap, matrix transform)23,000 generated cases per routine; calls in order, record bytes and the answer compared; 17 wrong versions, all caughtA stack word the transform stores is taken as zero; callees are scripted, not the sub-objects
Aim blend13,000 generated cases; calls, record bytes and answer compared; 8 wrong versions, all caughtThe hook's scratch argument is masked; the hook's answer is its three floats

Found (Verified). The transform stores a word its routine never writes: it is an uninitialised stack scratch in the original, and the checker's stack fill makes it zero. The lift stores zero and records this as a narrowing. Whether the game reads that word is open.

Found (Verified). The four tables share their flag bytes: table k, slot i reads the byte at k plus i, so the first table's second slot and the second table's first slot are the same byte.

Not reached. The zone list routine needs a larger memory window in the differential runtime than the runtime has. The other shapes were triaged by call counts and offsets only.

Written by lane l-free19; integrated by the coordinator.

entry.title: A fault blamed on an unrelocated read was undeclared callees, and a pass that depended on a mis-sized stack (lane a-H31)
entry.summary: Surprise 1 (Verified). A checker run that faulted on an unrelocated read was not a relocation problem. The relocation audit reported every absolute operand of the function relocated. The cause was native code: the probe's second argument took a polled-call block whose three callees had no declared stub or call-site patch, so the worker ran that original code directly and it jumped into an unrelocated address. Declaring the stubs (the same ones stage 20 used) and scripting the helper's answer as a valid heap object made the original complete 60 of 60.
entry.content:
Surprise 1 (Verified). A checker run that faulted on an unrelocated read was not a relocation problem. The relocation audit reported every absolute operand of the function relocated. The cause was native code: the probe's second argument took a polled-call block whose three callees had no declared stub or call-site patch, so the worker ran that original code directly and it jumped into an unrelocated address. Declaring the stubs (the same ones stage 20 used) and scripting the helper's answer as a valid heap object made the original complete 60 of 60.

Surprise 2 (Verified). A callee whose stack-word count is wrong does not show as an error in the stub; the run stalled. Setting the count to the six words the original pushes fixed it, and the stack check (esp) then passed on both sides.

Surprise 3 (Verified). A stage that matched by coincidence: the query threshold read the frame's scale word where the original reads the gate word. The mismatch appeared only after the stack count was corrected, so the earlier pass had been produced by the mis-sized stack.

Decision: the function stays deferred (partly_proven); steps 3, 4, 5 and the dl = 1 route in the rewrite are open. Probe s29r is in retry\probe for the next lane.

entry.title: An outside reverse-engineering toolkit evaluated from its documentation: not adopted, one idea taken
entry.summary: The owner asked whether REA, an open-source toolkit that gives AI agents reverse-engineering tools over the Model Context Protocol, could speed this project up. A research agent read its documentation; nothing was installed or run. The answer is that the product does not fit this project as it stands, and that its central idea is worth building here from what the project already has.
entry.content:
The owner asked whether REA, an open-source toolkit that gives AI agents reverse-engineering tools over the Model Context Protocol, could speed this project up. A research agent read its documentation; nothing was installed or run. The answer is that the product does not fit this project as it stands, and that its central idea is worth building here from what the project already has.

What was asked

Where do lanes lose time that a shared tool could save? Every lane that names a function or maps a large one first writes its own throwaway script to collect the same evidence: the strings a function references, its callers and callees, the class whose virtual table points at it, the names of its neighbours. A naming lane spends 10 to 30 minutes on that before it names anything, and sixty lanes do it at once.

What was found

QuestionWhat the documentation saysStatus
Can it use the project's analysed disassembler project?No. Each session imports a private copy of the binary into a temporary project and analyses it again; it never opens an existing project.Verified from its installation and provider pages.
Does it work on this machine?Its Windows support is described as experimental, read-only and for x64 hosts. This machine is an ARM64 host running x64 tools under emulation, which the documentation does not mention.Verified for what it says; unknown for this machine.
Can many lanes share it?Not stated. Each connection starts its own analysis engine with a default heap of 2 GB.Inferred: sixty lanes would each pay an import and a virtual machine.
Can it dump evidence for many functions in one run?No batch command is documented. Batch decompilation exists as an agent tool inside one session; a session's evidence can be exported once and read later without the engine.Verified for what is documented; three reference pages could not be read.
Does it help name functions that reference no strings?No similar-function search, no library signature matching, and no virtual-table or type-information recovery for Windows programs are documented.Verified as absent from the pages read.
Does its showcase's verification apply here?The showcase that runs thousands of cases against original code uses a harness written by the case study's author, not part of the toolkit.Verified. This project's checker already does more.
Stability and set-upFive releases with breaking changes in one week; set-up edits agent configuration for the user account, not per project.Verified.

What was decided

  • Not adopted. Nothing was installed.
  • The idea taken: one shared, queryable source of evidence for every lane. A tool lane is building one database for all game functions from the mapped image (calls, data references, strings, virtual tables, names, neighbours, and a simple signature for finding instances of one routine), with a script that prints a compact dossier per function. It holds no disassembly and no decompiler output and stays in the build area. Once proven on a real naming list it goes into the naming, production and large-function briefs.
  • For the owner to decide: the project's own disassembler could export pseudocode and basic-block listings for every function in one unattended run, kept out of the repository as all decompiler output is. That is several hours of processor time and has not been started.

What was confusing

An export of the call graph and cross-references made on 3 October was on disk all along (30,900 functions, 79,000 call pairs, 151,000 references) and no brief pointed lanes at it. It is older than the inventory and misses about 6,500 functions, so the new database is built from the image and checked against it.

entry.title: Three questions about the checker settled in a day, and an audit that withdrew two verified rewrites
entry.summary: Three things that lanes reported about the checker on 11 October were each given to an investigation lane before anyone acted on them. Two came back settled inside twenty minutes of work. The third, an audit of how verified rewrites convert floats to integers, found a real fault: two verified rewrites were withdrawn the same afternoon, and 288 more functions are being tested.
entry.content:
Three things that lanes reported about the checker on 11 October were each given to an investigation lane before anyone acted on them. Two came back settled inside twenty minutes of work. The third, an audit of how verified rewrites convert floats to integers, found a real fault: two verified rewrites were withdrawn the same afternoon, and 288 more functions are being tested.

A scripted callee's writes are the same on every call within a trial

What was asked: two lanes on two large functions (a file parser that reads a token per line, and a search loop that calls one callee per candidate) stopped on the belief that a scripted callee cannot write different words through its pointer argument on each call within a trial. Is that so?

FactStatusWhat it means
A callee's return value can follow a sequence that advances with each call inside a trial.Verified on the stock checker: a three-step sequence passes 200 of 200 where a once-per-trial answer fails 200 of 200.Use the per-call form for a callee that is called several times; use the per-trial form for one that is called once (an earlier entry records the opposite mistake).
The words a callee writes through a pointer are one row per trial.Verified from the worker's source and by experiment: each call writes the same words at its own destination. They do not depend on the call's index, on an argument, or on the call site for one stub.The two lanes were right about the limit.
What a lane can do today, with no change.Verified in a private copy, inferred for the stock build: a callee that returns a pointer can be given a sequence of pointers to different words, so its caller reads a different answer per call. Calls at different sites can have a stub each. A handler can be proven in a stage of its own with the token fixed for the trial.A stage with the token fixed proves that handler's code. It does not prove the transitions between handlers within one run, their order, or that one handler's exit state is valid for the next: those are listed as not covered.
A candidate extension: a per-call list of write rows.Built in a private copy only. Its regression contract fails to load on the stock driver and passes on the private build with a wrong version caught; the checker's own set gives identical verdicts on both builds for 61 of 62 contracts, the other being the absolute-read self-test that cannot run on this machine.Not adopted. It changes the worker and the driver, so it needs a checker review lane and a new checker version before any proof may use it.

The same lane found that the manual's line on scripted writes gives the count in the wrong unit: the count is in 32-bit words and the destination offset in bytes. An earlier lane lost an hour to exactly that.

The option for unrelocated absolute reads

Settled the same morning and recorded in its own entry: the option cannot set up on this machine. A follow-up worth recording here: the lane whose route seemed to need it ran the relocation checker on its function and found all 52 absolute operands relocated. The fault on that route has another cause, as every earlier claim of this kind had.

Float-to-integer conversions written with Rust's cast

What was asked: a lift lane noticed that two verified rewrites convert a float to an integer differently when the value is not a number or does not fit. The original's instruction gives a fixed result there; Rust's cast gives zero or the nearest end of the range. How many verified rewrites use the cast where the original's instruction behaves differently, and do their proofs cover those inputs?

FactValueStatus
Float-to-integer casts found326 certain, in 291 of 15,700 verified rewrites; 465 more that the detector could not type, not counted.Verified: a hand check of 30 flagged and 30 unflagged files found no false alarm and no miss on the final pass.
A random sample of 4028 are guarded in the rewrite so that it gives the processor's value; 5 agree on the bits that are used; 7 have no guard, in three functions.Verified for the 33; the 7 are unsettled.
The sevenThe lane's pairing of each cast with the original's instruction was unreliable, and a checker run on one of the three functions, whose contract should draw floats that overflow the cast, still passed 300 trials.Unknown: either the rewrite is wrong and the proof cannot see it, or the classification is wrong.
Estimate if the seven are realAbout 51 verified rewrites (25 to 93); about 7 if they are not.Inferred from the sample.

What was decided at first: nothing is withdrawn on an estimate. A second lane settled the three functions one by one: the original's conversion identified exactly by following the data, both sides computed on the special values, and any difference shown on the stock checker with a contract widened to reach them.

Settled the same afternoon

FunctionWhat the original doesResult on the stock checker
An audio query routine: six values converted and stored as 16-bit wordsA 32-bit truncating conversion, of which 16 bits are kept. For a positive value too large for 32 bits the original stores zero; the rewrite's cast stored the largest 16-bit value.Verified. The contract of record passes because its floats are small. With only two inputs steered out of range, the tracked rewrite fails 439 of 1,000 trials; a corrected conversion passes 1,000 of 1,000 with the old form failing as the wrong version. Withdrawn.
A small task routine: one value converted through a 64-bit integer storeAn x87 store of a 64-bit integer under truncation, of which the low half is used. The two sides differ only for positive infinity and values too large for 64 bits.Verified. With a global the game fills at run time steered that high, the tracked rewrite fails 67 of 1,000; the corrected form passes. Withdrawn. Whether the game can produce such a value there is unknown.
A fill routine with five conversionsFive 32-bit truncating conversions whose operands the code itself bounds: a counter that never exceeds 64.Verified safe. An instrumented run logged 24,984 operands, all in range. Not withdrawn.

The first lane's puzzle is explained: the proof that passed with inputs that "should overflow" never drew such inputs; its float cycles were small. That is the general lesson. A contract's ordinary float ranges do not reach the values on which a cast and an instruction differ, so a proof with ordinary ranges says nothing about them.

What was decided

  • The two rewrites are withdrawn; the verified count went down by two, with the reason in the changelog. A strengthening lane is proving the corrected copies with the contract of record and the widened contract together.
  • Production, queue and large-function briefs now carry the rule: a float is never converted with a bare cast unless the code bounds it first; otherwise the conversion is written to match the instruction, and the function's contract must reach not-a-number, the infinities and values past each end of the range, with a wrong version that uses the bare cast.
  • A scripted version of the widened test is being built and run over the other 288 functions that have such a cast. A pass counts only if the special values are shown to have reached the cast. The verified count may go down again.

How to reproduce

The two audit lanes' folders hold the detector for such casts, the list of 326, the classified sample, the widened contracts, the corrected rewrites, and the two conversion functions with their bit-level references and tests.

entry.title: Six operating faults of one night, five of them in the coordinator's own tooling
entry.summary: This entry records what went wrong in running the lanes between the evening of 10 October and the afternoon of 11 October, so that the next coordinator does not find each of them again. None of them produced a false result. Together they cost about nine hours of machine time.
entry.content:
This entry records what went wrong in running the lanes between the evening of 10 October and the afternoon of 11 October, so that the next coordinator does not find each of them again. None of them produced a false result. Together they cost about nine hours of machine time.

What happenedCauseWhat was changed
The machine went into standby from 07:06 to 11:33 and from 13:06 to 15:16. Nothing was verified for eight hours. Four Haiku lanes failed for want of a network and every background window ended at once.Verified from the system's power events. The request that keeps the machine awake is held by the coordinator's session and lapses when the session has been idle for five minutes. One interrupted turn of the coordinator was enough.The request was renewed and everything restarted; the lanes of the other model survived the standby and resumed by themselves. A hold on sleep that does not depend on the coordinator's session is the owner's decision and has been put to him.
Naming stood still for five hours with 1,300 functions unnamed and no naming lane running.Verified. The second naming pass left alone any function handed out in the last twelve hours, in case its lane was still running. After a burst of 35 naming lanes that covered nearly all of what was left, so the pass saw nothing to do. Naming had also been left out of the rotation of lane kinds.The pass asks the lane's log whether it is still running. Naming is in the rotation. The final pass uses small batches and tells each lane to read every function in full, since a survey of strings and neighbours had already failed on them.
The coordinator's re-run of a finished lane's proofs broke without cause, several times in the night, and one lane's twice in a row.Verified. The watchdog that stops processes left behind by ended lanes matched the re-run itself, because the re-run names the ended lane's contract. A broken re-run imports nothing and holds nothing, so nothing false was recorded.The watchdog skips any process whose command line names the coordinator's own folder.
Regression lanes were about to be told there was nothing left to re-run.Verified. See the entry on the regression runner: proofs handed to a lane and never reached counted as taken for good.What an ended lane did not reach is handed out again.
With sixty and more lanes, output fell to half of what thirty produced, and the coordinator's own commands took ten minutes.Measured over four hours: about 19,000 bytes of newly verified code an hour at about sixty lanes against 25,000 to 51,000 at thirty. The machine has 18 logical processors; memory was never the limit.Lanes of the other model and the regression runner run below normal priority; two finishers work the list of ended lanes from both ends, each lane claimed before it is worked on. The lane count itself is the owner's decision: he has chosen to fill memory, and each hour's figure is reported so the effect can be seen.
A lane left a search running over every lane folder for eighty minutes; another lane's command reached 3.2 GB.Verified. A recursive search of the whole scratch tree (2,500 folders) started by a lane and abandoned when its command timed out.The first was stopped by hand, by process id; the second by the guard that stops a project process above 3 GB. Lane prompts for investigation lanes now say never to search the whole scratch tree.

Signs worth knowing

  • A Haiku lane can hang with nothing running and no notice. The sign: no log line for fifteen minutes, no process whose command line names the lane, and no new file in its folder. Stop it and resume it with its context; if it hangs again, start a fresh session in the same folder with a short finishing prompt.
  • A lane of the other model that writes nothing to its lane log for half an hour is usually working: its own session log is the thing to look at.
  • After a standby, runs that were in progress are void: the drivers' time limits expire and the re-run records a timeout, which holds the claim until it is cleared and repeated.

entry.title: Old proofs are now re-run by a script, and the list of what was left had been wrong
entry.summary: About 13,700 functions are recorded as verified on an earlier version of the checker. Re-running each proof of record unchanged on the current checker, with its wrong version, is the regression the plan calls for. Until this morning lanes did it, slowly. A tool lane turned it into a script in 43 minutes, and wiring the script in showed that the process had been about to run out of work it could see.
entry.content:
About 13,700 functions are recorded as verified on an earlier version of the checker. Re-running each proof of record unchanged on the current checker, with its wrong version, is the regression the plan calls for. Until this morning lanes did it, slowly. A tool lane turned it into a script in 43 minutes, and wiring the script in showed that the process had been about to run out of work it could see.

What was asked

Six regression lanes settled 27 to 95 proofs each of the 350 each was given, in a hundred minutes: about 80 an hour for the project, a week for the backlog. Each lane wrote its own preparation, build and run scripts before running anything. Can the mechanical part be one resumable tool that needs no model?

What was found

FactValueWhat it means
The runner on its 123 test functions123 hold, every wrong version rejected, about 13 seconds a function with three workers. Stopped by process id in mid-run and restarted, it skipped what was settled and repeated nothing.Verified. The tool builds tracked rewrites in crates of thirty (a crate that fails is split in half, so one bad file costs only itself), runs each contract of record on the stock driver in a process of its own with a time limit, then the saved wrong version at 100 trials.
Its first full list: 350 proofs first recorded on checker version 5311 hold; 33 pass but have no saved wrong version; 5 could not run; 1 fails.Verified. The 311 are recorded on the current checker. The one that fails goes to the queue of old proofs that do not hold.
Proofs first recorded on checker versions 1 to 45,395 functions. Of 350 tried: 83 pass unchanged, with no wrong version to run; 2 hold.Verified. A wrong version per function was not required until version 5. These need one written, which is a lane's work; the runner can do the build and the thousand trials first.
The list maker for regression lanesIt reported 1,636 proofs left to hand out. 13,700 were still to re-run.Verified. It counted every proof ever handed to a regression lane as taken for good, and lanes reached a quarter of what they were given. After the correction it sees 6,857: what an ended lane did not reach is handed out again.

Three faults in the tool, found on real lists and corrected

  • Rewrites of the first weeks name the runtime's macros without a path, because their proving crates imported them at the crate root. The tool's crates did not, and 257 of 350 early rewrites failed to build for that one reason.
  • Some lanes' tracked rewrites carry their wrong version in the same file. The tool added the lane's saved copy as well, the name was defined twice, the build failed, and the tool dropped the wrong version and reported that none was saved: 19 of the first 30 proofs of one list.
  • The tool recorded what it could not settle as deferred. Its first list would have put 348 verified functions into the deferral queues as if they had failed. Such rows are now written as not reached, with the reason; the rows of that first list were corrected before anything imported them.

What was decided

  • The runner works through the proofs recorded on versions 5 to 7 (5,599 functions) in lists of 150, one list after another, below normal priority; the coordinator's import records each hold.
  • Regression lanes take the proofs without a wrong version, oldest first.
  • Nine proofs that a lane had recorded as unable to run (its worker was lost on them) hold under the runner; they are not counted until they have run once more.

What went wrong

In its first hour the runner ran at normal priority beside thirty production lanes that run below normal, and the hour's newly verified code halved. A re-run of old proofs must not take the processor from new work.

How to reproduce

The runner, its wrapper and the loop that makes lists and imports them are in the coordinator's scratch folder; the tool lane's folder has the agreement table against two regression lanes and the stop-and-resume test.

entry.title: Eight large functions closed in one night, and what each close taught about proofs
entry.summary: Between the evening of 10 October and the afternoon of 11 October, Claude Haiku 5.5 lanes closed eight functions of 2,200 to 4,500 bytes that lanes of the other model had left partly proven in stages: 26,000 bytes of code in all. None closed in one session; they took one to five sessions each. The coordinator re-ran every one before importing it. Five of the eight were sent back at least once after being reported as verified, and the reasons for sending them back are the useful part of this entry.
entry.content:
Between the evening of 10 October and the afternoon of 11 October, Claude Haiku 5.5 lanes closed eight functions of 2,200 to 4,500 bytes that lanes of the other model had left partly proven in stages: 26,000 bytes of code in all. None closed in one session; they took one to five sessions each. The coordinator re-ran every one before importing it. Five of the eight were sent back at least once after being reported as verified, and the reasons for sending them back are the useful part of this entry.

What was asked

The owner's rule of 10 October: Haiku lanes take the higher difficulties when the other model is struggling. The question for the night was whether a function left in stages can be closed at all, and what a lane must be told to do it.

What was found

FindingStatusWhat it means for the next lane
A wrong version that passes is a fault in the contract, not a limitation to list.Verified. A lane reported a function verified while listing that a version with one subtraction reversed still passed. Sent back to find out why, it found in six minutes that its 47 contracts placed a table of floats at the wrong address (the image address had not been turned into an offset from the image base), so the table read as zero on both sides and everything multiplied by it vanished.When a wrong version passes, find out why before anything else: a fixture at the wrong address, a value multiplied by a zero fill, cycles of equal length that pair two paths, a word that no check compares. Every lane's brief now says so.
A function with unwritten branches is not verified, however good the proof of the rest.Verified. One rewrite was reported verified with nine deliberate faults in it, seven marked as not written. Sent back, the lane showed by experiment that five of the seven are paths on which the original itself faults (it dereferences a null it was just handed), and wrote and proved the other two.Each deliberate fault left in a rewrite is classified: a path the original faults on or can never take, with the evidence, may stay and is listed; a path the original completes must be written and proven.
"Partly proven" can mean untested inputs, not unwritten code.Verified. A lane ended with a 4,490-byte function recorded as partly proven and a list of open items. A fresh session asked to classify them found that none was unwritten code: they were combinations of inputs passing through code already proven on other inputs, and two branches the original can never take. The function closed in 17 minutes.Before a function is left as partly proven, the question is asked of every open item: is it code that is not there, or inputs that were not run? Only the first keeps a function open; the second is listed as a narrowing.
The published rewrite must not carry its wrong versions.Verified. Two lanes kept their wrong versions as switches inside the function body (sixteen in one file). The file was folded to its correct arms, rebuilt, and re-proven before import; the wrong versions stay in a second build.One export, no wrong-version parameter, and the clean file is the one the clean build compiled, byte for byte.
An earlier stage can be wrong and still pass.Verified, several times: a callee modelled as writing nothing when it increments the count a later loop reads; a contract that pinned two values equal so that reading the wrong one could not show; a contract in which half the trials faulted identically on both sides and proved nothing; a probe that never reached a route because one scripted lookup always answered zero.Re-run the inherited stages on your own build first, then distrust them where your new stage disagrees. A trial that faults on both sides is not a pass: the original must complete.
The coordinator's re-run must read a proof in the form the lane kept it.Verified. One function was held by the re-run for a reason of form: its wrong versions were kept as 33 contracts of their own, each identical to a passing contract except for the library and the export, and the re-run read them as failing claims. The re-run now recognises such pairs by content and requires the wrong one to fail on a comparison.Either form is accepted: a wrong version declared in the contract, or a paired contract that differs only in library and export.

What worked as a way of briefing

  • An ordered list of small routes where the function is mapped; one narrow job where it is not (a frame map by experiment, one loop pass, one block built call by call against a probe that checks the first mismatch has moved); a checker investigation lane before anyone believes a reported checker fault.
  • Sending a lane back with the open items in order works: lanes stopped with most of their time unused in most first sessions, and continued when told what was left.
  • When a lane has grown long and stalls, a fresh session in the same lane folder with a short finishing prompt (reproduce the logged runs, replace the stale files, record the result) finished two functions in 10 and 17 minutes.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two functions took six and seven sessions and are still open, one with five routes left. The same belief about the checker stopped two lanes on two functions (see the entry on scripted writes). A lane session can hang with nothing running and no notice: the sign is no log line, no process of the lane's own and no new file for fifteen minutes.

How to reproduce

The briefing forms are in the coordinator's scratch folder as the per-lane additions to the queue brief; each closed function's lane folder holds its stage contracts, wrong versions and verdicts, and the coordinator's re-run of each is beside them.

entry.title: Lift: task block, turn, aim, flag, entry and record-scan routines (ped_task group, eight shapes)
entry.summary: Asked. Lift the 118 verified routines named as the ped task group that the earlier lane had not settled, grouped by the data they share rather than by name, one shape at a time, each lifted routine proven against its verified 32-bit rewrite.
entry.content:
Asked. Lift the 118 verified routines named as the ped task group that the earlier lane had not settled, grouped by the data they share rather than by name, one shape at a time, each lifted routine proven against its verified 32-bit rewrite.

Found (Verified). The names do not match the structures. Four names are shared by different routines: the aim update (four routines), the range check (two), the heading update (two) and the state initialiser (two). Grouping by what the rewrites read and write through their first argument gives eight shapes that could be lifted with a small owned type each, a set of forwarders with constant arguments, a set of routines whose target is computed from an index, and a set of routines that walk several objects. Nine routines in eight shapes were lifted; the rest is listed by reason in the lane's results.

ShapeRoutines liftedProofLeft out, and why
One task object: two read-only predicates24 differential tests; 9 wrong versions caughtIndex-computed pool accessors (3); a forwarder
Task state block reset12 differential tests; 5 wrong versions caughtNone in the shape
Task block constructor (seven callees)12 differential tests; 6 wrong versions caughtA 170-entry preset id table (decision needed)
Turn tracker (two trigonometric callees)12 differential tests; 10 wrong versions caughtDouble-precision callee (not callable from stable Rust)
Typed-record table scan12 differential tests; 7 wrong versions caughtA link-chain range check (two hops) and a global-row range check
Aim record update (two collaborators)12 differential tests; 7 wrong versions caughtOther aim updates (different objects)
Owner subject-flag update (six collaborators)12 differential tests; 6 wrong versions caughtNone in the shape
Entry initialiser (four collaborators)12 differential tests; 6 wrong versions caughtNone in the shape

Finding (Verified). Two verified rewrites in this group convert a float to an integer in different ways. The block constructor's rewrite uses the Rust conversion, which gives zero for a not-a-number and saturates outside the signed 32-bit range. The entry initialiser's rewrite gives the processor's truncating result, the most negative integer, for both. The lift of each follows its own rewrite. For the block constructor the difference cannot arise in the game: the two factors it reads from the image are one over 2^15 and minus 500, so the product stays between minus 500 and zero for any sixteen-bit draw. The proof of each shows the difference is measured, not assumed.

Finding (Verified). In the aim update, a not-a-number first direction component kept a different sign in the lift until the operand order of the single-precision operations was pinned with the same opaque-operand helper the rewrite uses. The rewrite was not changed.

Finding (Inferred). One routine copies a 170-entry preset table into the task system. The table is game data, so copying it into tracked source needs a decision; it is left out.

Decided. Each shape gets its own owned type, named for its data, in a separate module: none of the shapes shares a structure, so no single class was lifted. Collaborators travel as one trait per routine; their constant arguments are supplied by the implementation, and the proof compares the calls in order with their arguments. Callee-written scratch words are compared as non-null tokens; the proof does not compare their contents. Wrong versions each change one thing, and the proof prints how often each wrong version differs from its rewrite.

How to reproduce. Build the eight differential test programs of the test crate for the 32-bit target and run them one at a time; then run the host tests of the peds-tasks crate on the 64-bit host. The include paths in the test crate are local to the lane's scratch tree and are shortened by the integration script.

entry.title: A probe pin that answered zero hid a whole route
entry.summary: What was asked: a lane probe had to get the original to call a new helper on at least 20 of 60 completed trials, and the probe had been run for 60 trials with the helper's call site stubbed. It never fired the helper.
entry.content:
What was asked: a lane probe had to get the original to call a new helper on at least 20 of 60 completed trials, and the probe had been run for 60 trials with the helper's call site stubbed. It never fired the helper.

What was found (Verified): the probe scripted the lookup callee that the original calls just before the helper (a state-word record lookup) to answer zero. The original then takes a different branch and never reaches the helper. Scripting that one callee to answer a record on odd trials made the helper fire on 30 of 60 trials. The probe had been pinned on the object words and the other callees, and the lookup callee was the one that had been missed.

What it means: when a probe shows a route vacuous, check the scripted answer of every callee on the route before concluding the route is unreachable. A cycled script indexes by trial number, so a branch that only odd trials reach needs an odd index in its script.

Also (Verified): a helper answer and a region object answer scripted on the wrong parity left the branch unreached for a whole probe run, and a callee whose call site was left unpatched ran the real code natively.

How to reproduce: the probe contract and its generator are in the lane's retry folder (mkprobe.py, contracts28).
